body.text: The first time I landed at Henderson Field, in 2012, Honiara felt a very long way from anywhere.

In 1942, this strip of tropical runway sat at the center of the battle for Guadalcanal, where Japan’s seemingly unstoppable southern advance across the Pacific finally began to run the other way. The six-month campaign was brutal, fought across land, sea and air, and cost tens of thousands of lives.

Seventy years later, the airport seemed barely to have moved on from the World War II era. You walked off the plane into the blazing sun and across the tarmac to a low, tired terminal. Above arrivals, behind a fence, the viewing area was packed with people. There seemed to be far more of them than could conceivably have been waiting for passengers from our flight.

Inside, immigration delivered perhaps the most irritating adoption of Western bureaucracy: the handwritten arrival card. After flying thousands of kilometers to a tropical island, apparently the first order of business was to find a pen and write down information already contained in your passport.

Outside, a collection of dusty SUVs waited in the heat. A group of young men, wearing very little, danced and played panpipes for the new arrivals. It was hard to know whether this was a cultural welcome, tourist theater, or something somewhere in between.
Then came the drive into Honiara. The road was narrow and badly potholed. Small houses sat beside it among dust, rubbish, and dogs. People walked along the roadside.

Eventually this gave way to Honiara itself: a low strip of shops and government buildings stretched between the mountains and the sea. Betel-nut stains covered the ground. People gathered along the roadside, chewing betel nuts and talking. There was no particular sense that anyone was in a hurry.

There was basically one hotel you wanted to stay in. The air conditioning leaked, the bed creaked, and the windows never quite shut. The Wi-Fi came on little prepaid cards that charged by the hour. Actually getting an hour of it required standing on one leg on a table in the corner of your room.

It did, however, have an excellent Japanese restaurant. Some 70 years after Japanese and Allied warships had fought one another in the waters off Guadalcanal, this seemed a modest but welcome reconciliation.
Things moved slowly in Honaira. Government officials sometimes didn’t turn up for meetings. Sometimes entire ministries seemed to be empty, with nobody inside. Nobody.

Back in 2012, the Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands (RAMSI) was winding down. Or at least everyone kept saying it was winding down. The discussion then was about what happened next. Could the institutions survive once the outsiders left? Would everything that had been built actually last?
Eventually RAMSI did leave, and to the rest of the world, Honiara disappeared from most people’s attention. But not for very long.
Fourteen years and something like 20 visits later, I landed at Henderson Field again. The panpipe dancers were gone.
Ironically, the Japanese have built part of a new airport terminal. Departures is now all glass, air-conditioning, and modern efficiency. Arrivals, on the other hand, retains much of its old charm.

The road into town is smooth. Whether it is more pleasant is debatable, because there are now thousands more cars trying to use it. Where there was once dust, scattered houses, and empty roadside, shops, businesses and buildings now crowd much of the way into Honiara.

Driving around has become a game of donor bingo: Look for the flag. Chinese funding built a football stadium and swimming pool for the Pacific Games. Australia, Japan, New Zealand, and others have their names attached to projects around town. Everybody seems to be building something, funding something or opening something.

When I arrived, two private jets were parked on the tarmac. Out in the harbor I see a yacht reportedly worth $37 million. Within a week, the jets and the yacht were gone. That is one of the peculiarities of modern Honiara: the capital city looks wealthier, but Solomon Islands isn’t.

Former U.S. President George W. Bush once joked about the “haves and the have-mores” at a charity dinner – a line Michael Moore later put to rather different use in “Fahrenheit 9/11,” minus the joke’s original context. Honiara increasingly feels like a city of the have-mores and the have-nots.
And that contradiction is considerably more interesting than another argument about who is “winning” the Pacific.

Solomon Islands has become important. A country of fewer than a million people has found itself in the middle of a much larger argument about the future of the Pacific. Security agreements, policing, diplomatic visits, money, infrastructure: suddenly everybody cares about the government’s decisions.
There is a temptation to imagine Solomon Islands as a chessboard. It isn’t, and Solomon Islanders are not pieces.

The political elite know perfectly well what is happening around them. Many have studied overseas. Ministers and senior officials understand the strategic anxieties of the countries competing for their attention. Why wouldn’t they take advantage of it? If several countries suddenly decide that your friendship matters enormously, taking what is on offer is hardly irrational. Picking a side, however, might be.

Much of the outside commentary therefore gets Solomon Islands backwards. The question is invariably what Solomon Islands means for everybody else. A better question is what everybody else suddenly means for Solomon Islands.

Solomon Islands routinely talks about tourism as part of its economic future. It should; the country is gorgeous. There are jungle-covered islands dropping straight into water so clear you can see the reef below, empty beaches, wrecks from the Pacific War and some of the best diving on earth.

Yet barely anyone comes. That might seem like a mystery, until you actually try to visit. For roughly the cost of a holiday in Sydney or Fiji, Solomon Islands offers fewer flights, fewer hotels, higher prices, and considerably less certainty that anything will work as advertised.

There are some wonderful contradictions in modern Honiara. One of them its that Solomon Islands struggles to turn its existing advantages into something people can easily use. That problem extends well beyond tourism.

Heritage Park Hotel, where many of the visiting diplomats, consultants and officials stay, now reportedly generates around 95 percent of its own electricity from solar. But this isn’t a case of environmental idealism; it is pragmatism at its finest. There is something almost perfect about one of Honiara’s premier hotels deciding that one of the country’s basic utilities works better if it largely provides it itself.

In Solomon Islands, electricity prices are among the highest in the world. More than a third of households have no electricity at all. For those that do, being connected and being able to afford to use it are two rather different things.
You can see versions of that contradiction all over Honiara. There is more money around. More cars. More people flying in and out. It is less obvious how much has changed in people’s everyday life.

Australia, in particular, has spent an enormous amount of time and money in Solomon Islands. RAMSI was one of its largest and longest regional interventions. Canberra has supported Solomon Islands’ elections, policing, and government for decades. There are good reasons for that. A peaceful, democratic Solomon Islands is good for Australia.

It is also, rather obviously, good for Solomon Islanders. Democracy won’t create jobs or make hundreds of scattered islands easier to govern. But elections matter. Laws matter. Government matters. Most of all, it matters whether a government can actually do what it says it is going to do.

Australia’s relationship with Solomon Islands has been built over decades: Australians and Solomon Islanders working alongside one another in ministries, police stations, hospitals, and schools; Solomon Islanders studying in Australia; families, churches, universities, businesses, and communities connecting the two countries. None of it is particularly flashy, but that is rather the point.

Then there are Solomon Islands’ constituency development funds: money ostensibly for development, although “development” has proved a wonderfully elastic concept. School fees, funerals, roofing iron – the definition has stretched to meet the occasion. Not all are classic entries in the development handbook.

Australia has spent decades putting money into the harder, slower work of building institutions and services. Yet according to a recently leaked message, it is now proposing millions for every constituency.

That money won’t strengthen the institutions Australia has spent years helping to build. It will instead go around them, into a system built around individual MPs. Foreign assistance may start looking remarkably like formalized slush funds with a development label. In trying to secure the relationship, Australia risks entrenching precisely the kind of transactional politics it has spent years trying to move beyond.

But the problem with transactional relationships is that eventually someone else turns up with more to offer Australia’s strongest advantage in Solomon Islands has never really been the size of its check. It is time.
Guadalcanal spreads beneath every plane that departs Henderson Field. Upon seeing the island, it is difficult not to think about time.

More than 80 years ago, outsiders came to these islands because Solomon Islands suddenly mattered to a Pacific war. Henderson Field became something to be captured and defended. Ships sank in the waters off Honiara. Thousands of foreigners arrived, fought, built, died, and eventually left.
Solomon Islanders remained.
Fourteen years ago, the question was what would happen when another collection of outsiders left. RAMSI wound down; attention moved elsewhere; again, Solomon Islanders remained.

Now the outsiders are back. Nobody sensible is predicting another Guadalcanal campaign, of course. But once again these islands have acquired an importance largely explained through the ambitions and anxieties of people somewhere else.
Solomon Islands hasn’t changed, in governance or geography. What has changed is how much everyone else suddenly cares about it – and who Solomon Islands chooses to call its friends. For now.

The private jets will leave. The yacht will sail away. Governments elsewhere will change. Strategic priorities will shift. Today’s indispensable partnership will eventually compete with tomorrow’s crisis.

Solomon Islanders, as always, will stay. They were here during the Pacific campaign. They were here before RAMSI arrived and after RAMSI left. They are here for today’s new Pacific contest. They will be here for whatever comes next.
That is the thing outsiders have repeatedly failed to understand about Solomon Islands. Everyone else gets to go home when their mission is complete.
